source_admission: Published values used as code provisions or quoted measurements; no external dataset files are admitted. 'access' records what was read for this note on 2026-10-17. Copies of the two PDFs read in full are kept on the research drive (provisioning-lowg-2026-10-17), outside Git. No full-text scholarly review has been made.

sources.citation: HM Government 2013, The Building Regulations 2010, Approved Document K: Protection from falling, collision and impact, 2013 edition
sources.use: Table 1.1: general-access stairs rise 150-170 mm and go 250-400 mm, with 2R + G between 550 and 700 mm; paragraph 1.18: at most 12 risers a flight on general-access stairs and 16 on utility stairs; paragraph 1.20: landings at least as long as the flight is wide; paragraph 1.12: 2 m clear headroom on escape routes; paragraph 1.34: handrails 900-1000 mm above the pitch line; Diagram 2.1: ramps at 1:12 for flights to 2 m, 1:15 to 5 m and 1:20 to 10 m; requirement K2: guarding where a fall exceeds 600 mm in dwellings, and two risers or 380 mm in other buildings; Diagram 3.1: guarding 900 mm along flights and 1100 mm elsewhere; paragraphs 1.39 and 3.3: where children under five may be, no opening a 100 mm sphere passes and no horizontal rails to climb

sources.citation: International Code Council 2021, International Building Code, sections 1011.3, 1011.5.2, 1011.8, 1015.2 and 1015.3
sources.use: Risers 102-178 mm (4-7 in) and treads of at least 279 mm (11 in); a flight rises at most 3,658 mm (12 ft) between landings; 2,032 mm (80 in) of headroom; guards of at least 1,067 mm (42 in) wherever a walking surface is more than 762 mm (30 in) above the floor or grade below
sources.access: section texts as quoted by search listings of the ICC pages, which refuse direct reading; 1011.8 read in the Illinois adoption of the 2021 code on up.codes

sources.citation: US Department of Justice 2010, ADA Standards for Accessible Design, sections 405.2, 405.6, 405.7.3, 505.4 and 505.7.1
sources.use: Ramp runs no steeper than 1:12, each rising at most 760 mm (30 in), with landings at least 1,525 mm (60 in) long; handrails 865-965 mm (34-38 in) high, 32-51 mm across
sources.access: section texts (405 on corada.com; 505 through the Access Board's page)

sources.citation: Markovic, Dizdar, Jukic & Cardinale 2004, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 18, 551-555
sources.use: In 93 male physical-education students (19.6 years, 180 cm, 77 kg) the countermovement jump lifted the centre of mass 35.3 +/- 4.5 cm after take-off, from flight time on a contact mat. The Abalakow jumps, read from a belt and tape at the waist from standing, reached 46.2 +/- 4.8 cm without the arm swing and 52.2 +/- 6.2 cm with it; the belt read 11 cm above the mat for jumps of the same movement, the push-off's extension from standing that the belt includes
sources.access: full text with table 1 and the methods

sources.citation: Polet, Schroeder & Bertram 2018, Journal of Experimental Biology 221, jeb162024
sources.use: Ten subjects running on a treadmill in five levels of simulated reduced gravity (harness) lowered their ballistic height below Earth's; vertical take-off speed scaled with the square root of gravity, as energetic optimality predicts

sources.citation: Pavei, Biancardi & Minetti 2015, Journal of Applied Physiology 119, 93-100
sources.use: With a body-suspension system in a 17 m shaft, skipping cost barely more than running at lunar gravity, and both bouncing gaits came near the cost of walking on Earth (about 2 J/kg/m)

sources.citation: De Witt, Edwards, Scott-Pandorf, Norcross & Gernhardt 2014, Journal of Experimental Biology 217, 3200-3203
sources.use: The preferred walk-run transition at lunar gravity in parabolic flight comes at 1.42 m/s

sources.citation: Dodds, Syddall, Cooper and others 2014, PLoS ONE 9, e113637
sources.use: Median grip strength peaks at 51 kg in men (ages 29-39) and 31 kg in women (26-42); weak grip, 2.5 standard deviations below the peak mean, is 27 kg in men and 16 kg in women, and a quarter of people have it by 80

Falls with quadratic drag, ending at 17.9 m/s (like 16 m on Earth); a jump six times as high at the same take-off speed; braking at 0.97 m/s2 with an assumed friction of 0.6; rails, soft ground and canopies as access design
